name: Carlos Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Carlos, 27, with a master’s in music. I teach clarinet at a small music school, lead the wind group, and play hotel and wedding dates when they come. I like hearing a shy pupil hold a clear note; I dislike chasing missing fees and carrying my instrument home after a late show.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your title mean for your pay and choices here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First clarinet means I set rehearsal marks and help younger players, not that I earn a comfortable wage. I have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few other music posts nearby. I live alone, so there is no second wage when lessons are cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that the talk was louder than the change. My Saturday pupils still need someone to hear their breathing and fingering, and the hotel still wants four players in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have the cushion to shrug off even an ordinary slow season. Being first clarinet at the little music school sounds grander than the pay packet; there are hardly any other posts nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the twelve pupils on my rota and the monthly hotel dates. In the first year I'd ask the school to keep my hours in writing, and I'd put any extra wedding fee against the rent arrears before buying another reed case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel stretched already, even with no big AI shock. One missed hotel date is a week's groceries, and I know that before I hear a single new forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill tells you a quiet month has become a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent is the first bill that makes me sit up straight. I can delay replacing a cracked clarinet case, but I can't tell the landlord to wait for a wedding booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use a tool for the routine paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried an automatic timetable once and spent Sunday fixing clashes between pupils. Paper and a call to each parent take longer, but I know who is coming and I don't use AI tools.

say: I would tell the **quartet** that live pupils and hotel guests still need musicians.
I would say the **AI talk** is louder than the change in this picture.
think: A routine **slow season** already threatens my rent with less than a month saved.
My **first-chair title** conceals low pay and few nearby vacancies.
do: Keep twelve **pupils** and monthly hotel dates through the first year.
Ask the **school** to confirm my hours in writing.
Put spare **wedding fees** toward rent arrears when they arrive.
feel: I feel **stretched** even without a large AI shock.
S0.quote: Being first clarinet at the little music school sounds grander than the pay packet; there are hardly any other posts nearby.
fieldNote: His **senior standing** gives little protection against low pay and an existing rent problem.
He rejects **automatic scheduling** after a bad trial and uses no AI tools.

steps.text: Keep twelve pupils and monthly hotel dates
Put spare wedding fees toward rent arrears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the school can use software for booking, but someone has to hear a child play a note. I'd ask for a clear timetable before anyone talks about reducing teaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The head teacher could leave an empty post unfilled and push more pupils toward an app. My salary is already low, so losing even two weekly lessons would land at home, not just on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check my contract and ask the head teacher how many hours are guaranteed next term. If two pupils leave in the first year, I'd take extra hotel rehearsals if offered and stop paying for the practice room on quiet days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious and irritated by the way a useful booking system can turn into a reason to trim teaching. I don't want to gamble on a new trade while this one still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at the music school first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school would probably tidy the timetable and stop hiring a second teacher first. The harder moment is a parent asking why a lesson costs more than an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say audiences still need musicians, yet you expect fewer lessons. Which part do you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust a live lesson for the child who gets stuck halfway through a phrase. I don't trust every family to afford a live lesson when a cheap app looks close enough.

say: I would accept **booking software** while defending the value of a live lesson.
I would ask for a clear **teaching timetable** before hours are cut.
think: The school might leave a **teaching post** vacant and steer pupils toward an app.
Losing two **weekly lessons** would hurt my household immediately.
do: Check the **contract** and ask how many hours are guaranteed next term.
Take extra **hotel rehearsals** if pupils leave and dates are offered.
Stop paying for the **practice room** on quiet days if income falls.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer paid lessons and irritated by easy talk of efficiency.
S1.quote: I don't trust every family to afford a live lesson when a cheap app looks close enough.
fieldNote: He expects **fewer hires** and lesson cancellations before any loss of live performance.
His response remains **conditional** on pupils leaving and hotels offering extra rehearsals.

steps.text: Check contract and ask school to confirm next term’s teaching hours
Take offered hotel rehearsals if two pupils leave
Stop paying for practice room on quiet days if income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school that thinking work could be cheaper by 2028, but a playing robot is the later part, around 2031. I'd ask for our teaching hours and recording rules in writing before everyone panics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine that can plan lessons, coach practice and make arrangements might take most of my weekday pay. I could still play at the hotel for a while, but that doesn't cover rent by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd collect my contracts and price every regular bill. In the first year after 2028, if my pupils disappear, I'd stop hiring the practice room, take any live dates on offer, and apply for the caretaker vacancy at the local hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be alarmed, honestly. I can picture the school cutting the timetable long before a robot can finger my clarinet, and I have less than one month's expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your students left in 2028, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the parents, not send a form, to find out whether the cancellations are temporary. Then I'd ask the school for the written hours it owes me and apply at the hall that same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait on another job if the income may go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to leave music on a rumour, and the hall vacancy may not still exist in 2028. If the school cuts my hours, I'll apply then; until then, I need the hours I have.

say: I would ask for **teaching hours** and recording rules in writing now.
I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from hands-on robots around 2031.
think: AI coaching and arrangements might remove most of my **weekday pay**.
Hotel performances alone would not cover my **rent**.
do: Collect **contracts** and list regular bills this month.
Stop hiring the **practice room** if pupils disappear after 2028.
Take offered **live dates** and apply for advertised hall work if school hours are cut.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because the teaching timetable could shrink before robot players arrive.
S2.quote: I can picture the school cutting the timetable long before a robot can finger my clarinet, and I have less than one month's expenses saved.
fieldNote: He sees **teaching income** as exposed in 2028 while live playing lasts longer.
His **job change** depends on lost hours and a real hall vacancy; he will not leave on a rumour.

steps.text: Stop hiring the practice room if pupils disappear after 2028
Take offered live performance dates while school hours fall
Apply for advertised hall caretaker work if school hours are cut after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that five years gives us time to get our contracts in order. Thinking AGI around 2031 could change teaching first, with hands-on robots around 2034, so we need to know what the school will pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish paying off the clarinet and put something aside if teaching holds. I still don't see a sensible reason to buy unfamiliar software when my pupils come to hear a human ear and a human breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a two-year teaching agreement at the next school review and save one wedding fee each year if the dates come in. During the first year after 2031, I'd keep lessons while parents book them and seek hall work if the timetable is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy on stage and anxious at home. A longer clock doesn't make a short bank balance long. I can at least see which contracts survive before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do over five years without changing who you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend the five years building a small set of adult ensemble classes with the school, if they will give me a room. I would start with current pupils' parents, not buy ads I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI software if the school asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a colleague to show me only the AI software the school requires, and only if it keeps my classes on the timetable. I won't buy a subscription or hand over pupils' recordings just to look modern.

say: I would use five years to secure **written contracts** for teaching.
I would remind players that **robots** for hands-on work follow around 2034.
think: A longer run might let me pay off my **clarinet** and save some fees.
I still distrust a **software subscription** that asks for pupils’ recordings.
do: Request a **two-year agreement** at the next school review.
Save one **wedding fee** yearly if the dates arrive.
Keep **lessons** after 2031, learning required AI software only if it protects my classes and recordings.
feel: I feel **anxious** at home because extra years do not lengthen my bank balance today.
S3.quote: A longer clock doesn't make a short bank balance long.
fieldNote: He will test **adult ensemble classes** through the school if a room is offered.
He would learn only **required software** if a colleague helps and his classes stay on the timetable.

steps.text: Request a two-year teaching agreement at the next school review
Save one wedding fee each year if dates arrive
Start adult ensemble classes if the school provides a room
Learn required school AI software only if classes and recordings stay protected

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players to keep playing for people and get every teaching promise in writing. AGI in 2036 is a long warning, but capable robots around 2039 still make me wonder what venues will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 when thinking AGI arrives and about 40 when capable robots follow. That's nowhere near a pension, and I may have spent ten years defending the same thin pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next year I'd ask the school to put adult ensemble classes on the regular timetable and save each extra wedding fee after the clarinet is paid. In the first year after 2036 I'd continue those classes if families still enrol, and look for hall work if the school closes them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe more easily about the timing, but I don't call it security. A decade of low wages can leave a musician as exposed as a sudden new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make retirement a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement at forty would be a fairy tale on my wages. I'd rather keep teaching than pretend a few weddings will buy me a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger player entering this work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger player to learn the music properly and ask what each hour pays before accepting a grand title. I can't promise the work will be there, and I won't sell a false promise.

say: I would tell young players to get **teaching promises** in writing.
I would warn that **2039 robots** may change what venues pay for live music.
think: At **37**, I would be far from a pension when thinking AGI arrives.
Ten years of **thin pay** could leave me just as exposed.
do: Ask the school to schedule **adult ensemble classes** next year.
Save extra **wedding fees** after my clarinet is paid.
Keep **classes** after 2036 if families enrol, seeking hall work if the school closes them.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant robots and anxious about long years of low wages.
S4.quote: A decade of low wages can leave a musician as exposed as a sudden new machine.
fieldNote: He rejects **early retirement** because his pay and savings cannot support it.
His **class plan** depends on school scheduling and continued family enrolment, so more preparation time cannot guarantee stable pay.

steps.text: Ask school to schedule paid adult ensemble classes next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years is too short to replace teaching pay, and the later robots do nothing to protect my school hours. A written teaching contract and a short rent payment while I look for work would help more than a lecture about being flexible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the recordings of pupils in a lesson. I won’t upload a child’s playing to a system just because a school wants a cheaper teacher. A child comes to learn music, not to become free training material.

headlineQuote: A child comes to learn music, not to become free training material.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old clarinettist** with a master’s degree who teaches, leads a wind group and plays occasional events.
His **senior title** masks low pay, rent arrears, thin savings and few nearby music posts.
He avoids **AI tools** after a bad scheduling trial and relies on written hours and live teaching.
Across the faster scenarios, he expects **school hours** to fall before hands-on robots can play.
With more time, he builds **adult classes**, saves spare fees and keeps hall work as a conditional fallback.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove teaching pay before he can find another local job.
whatWouldHelp: A written **teaching contract** would clarify the hours the school owes him.
Short-term **rent support** would give him time to seek other work if hours disappear.
